exampleAnswers.title: Finding the First Term Exceeding a Given Value

question.text:
What is the first term that exceeds  $2\,000\,000$ in the following geometric sequence?
\[
\quad\quad\quad\quad 2,\: 2\sqrt 5,\: 10,\: 10\sqrt 5,\: \ldots
\]
question.explanation:
The first term of the sequence is $a_1=2$ and the common ratio is \[ r = \dfrac {2\sqrt 5} 2 = \sqrt 5. \]

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as

\begin{align*} a_n & = a_1 \cdot r ^{n -1}\\[5pt] & = 2 \cdot \left(\sqrt 5\right)^{n-1}\\[5pt] & = 2 \cdot 5^{(n - 1)/2}. \end{align*}

We want the $n$th term to be greater than $2\, 000\, 000.$ Hence,

\begin{align*} a_n &> 2\,000\,000 \\[5pt] 2 \cdot 5^{(n - 1)/2} & > 2\, 000\, 000\\[5pt] 5^{(n - 1)/2} & > 1\, 000\, 000\\[5pt] \log \left( 5^{(n - 1)/2} \right) & > \log (1\, 000\, 000)\\[5pt] \dfrac {(n - 1)}{2} \cdot \log (5) & > \log (1\, 000\, 000)\\[5pt] \dfrac {(n - 1)} 2 & > \dfrac {\log (1\, 000\, 000)} {\log (5)}\\[5pt] n - 1 & > \dfrac {2\log (1\, 000\, 000)} {\log (5)}\\[5pt] n & > \dfrac {2\log (1\, 000\, 000)} {\log (5)} + 1. \end{align*}

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

\[ \dfrac {2\log (1\, 000\, 000)} {\log (5)} + 1 \approx 18.168. \]

Therefore, the $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{19}$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $2\, 000\, 000.$

What is the first term that exceeds $58\,000$ in the following geometric sequence?
\[
2,\: 8,\: 32,\: 128,\: \ldots
\]

The first term of the sequence is $a_1=2$ and the common ratio is \[ r = \dfrac {8} {2} = 4. \]

We want the $n$th term to be greater than $58\, 000.$ Hence,

\begin{align*} a_n &> 58\,000 \\[5pt] 2 \cdot 4^{n-1} & > 58\, 000\\[5pt] 4^{n-1} & > 29\, 000\\[5pt] \log (4^{n-1} ) & > \log (29\,000)\\[5pt] (n - 1) \log (4) & > \log (29\,000)\\[5pt] n - 1 & > \dfrac {\log (29\, 000)} {\log (4)} \\[5pt] n & > \dfrac {\log (29\, 000)} {\log (4)} + 1. \end{align*}

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

\[ \dfrac {\log (29\, 000)} {\log (4)} + 1 \approx 8.412. \]

question.text:
What is the first term that exceeds  $1\,000$ in the following geometric sequence?
\[
\sqrt{2},\: 2,\: 2\sqrt{2},\: 4,\: \ldots
\]
question.explanation:
The first term of the sequence is $a_1=\sqrt{2}$ and the common ratio is \[ r = \dfrac {2}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}. \]

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as

\begin{align*} a_n & = a_1 \cdot r ^{n -1}\\[5pt] & = \sqrt{2} \cdot \left(\sqrt{2}\right)^{n-1}\\[5pt] & = 2^{n/2}. \end{align*}

We want the $n$th term to be greater than $1\,000.$ Hence,

\begin{align*} a_n &> 1\,000 \\[5pt] 2^{n/2} & > 1\, 000\\[5pt] \log \left( 2^{n/2} \right) & > \log (1\, 000) \\[5pt] \dfrac {n}{2} \cdot \log (2) & > \log (1\, 000) \\[5pt] \dfrac {n}{2} & > \dfrac {\log (1\,000)} {\log (2)} \\[5pt] n & > \dfrac {2\log (1\, 000)}{\log (2)}. \end{align*}

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

\[ \dfrac {2\log (1\, 000)} {\log (2)} \approx 19.932. \]

Therefore, the $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{20}$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $1\, 000.$

question.text: What is the first term that is less than $0. 001$ in the following geometric sequence? \[ 64,\: 48,\: 36,\: 27 ,\: \ldots \]
question.explanation:
The first term of the sequence is $a_1=64$ and the common ratio is \[ r = \dfrac{48}{64} = \dfrac{3}{4}. \]

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as:

\begin{align*} a_n & = a_1 \cdot r ^{n -1}\\[5pt] & = 64 \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^{n-1} \end{align*}

We want the $n$th term to be less than $ 0. 001.$ Hence:

\begin{align*} a_n & < 0.001 \\[5pt] 64 \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^{n-1} & < 0.001\\[5pt] \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^{n-1} & < \dfrac{0.001}{64}\\[5pt] \log \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^{n-1} & < \log (0. 000\, 016)\\[5pt] (n-1) \log \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right) & < \log (0. 000\, 016)\\[5pt] n-1 & > \dfrac{\log (0. 000\, 016)}{\log\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)}\\[5pt] n & > \dfrac{\log (0. 000\, 016)}{\log\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)}+1 \end{align*}

Note that we reversed the inequality sign when divided by $\log\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)$ because $\log\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)$ is a negative number.

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

\[ \dfrac{\log (0. 000\, 016)}{\log\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)}+1 \approx 39.386 \]

Therefore, the $40$th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than $0. 001.$

question.text:
What is the first term that is less than $0. 000\, 000\,5$ in the following geometric sequence?
\[
\quad\quad\quad\quad 256,\: 64,\: 16,\: 4,\: \ldots
\]
question.explanation:
The first term of the sequence is $a_1=256$ and the common ratio is

\[ r = \dfrac{64}{256} = \dfrac{1}{4}. \]

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as

\begin{align*} a_n & = a_1 \cdot r ^{n -1}\\[5pt] & = 256 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{n-1}\\[5pt] & = 4^4 \cdot 4^{1-n}\\[5pt] & = 4^{5-n}. \end{align*}

We want the $n$th term to be less than $ 0. 000\,000\,5.$ Hence,

\begin{align*} a_n & < 0.000\,000\,5 \\[5pt] 4^{5-n} & < 0.000\, 000\,5\\[5pt] \log \left(4^{5-n}\right) & < \log (0. 000\, 000\,5)\\[5pt] (5-n)\log \left(4\right) & < \log (0. 000\, 000\,5)\\[5pt] 5-n & < \dfrac{\log (0. 000\, 000\,5)}{\log (4)}\\[5pt] -n & < \dfrac{\log (0. 000\, 000\,5)}{\log (4)} - 5\\[5pt] n & > 5 - \dfrac{\log (0. 000\, 000\,5)}{\log (4)} . \end{align*}

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

\[ 5 - \dfrac{\log (0. 000\, 000\,5)}{\log (4)} \approx 15.466 . \]

Therefore, the $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{16}$th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than $0. 000\,000\, 5.$

question.text: The $3$rd term of a geometric sequence is $18$, and the $6$th term is $486.$ The first term of this sequence to exceed $10\,000$ is the
question.explanation:
Since we are given that $a_3=18$ and $a_6=486$, we can find the common ratio $r$ of the sequence, as follows:

\begin{align*} r^{n-m} & = \dfrac{a_n}{a_m} \\[5pt] r^{6-3} & = \dfrac{a_6}{a_3} \\[5pt] r^3 &=\dfrac{486}{18} \\[5pt] r^3 &= 27 \\[5pt] r &= 3 \end{align*}

Now, since $a_{3}= 18$ and $r= 3$, we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for $a_1$, as follows:

\begin{align*} a_n &=a_1\cdot r^{n-1} \\[3pt] a_3 &=a_1\cdot 3^{3-1} \\[3pt] 18 &=a_1\cdot 3^2 \\[3pt] 18 &= 9 a_1 \\[3pt] a_1 &= 2 \end{align*}

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

\begin{align*} a_n & = a_1 \cdot r ^{n -1} \\[5pt] & = 2 \cdot 3^{n - 1}. \end{align*}

We want $n$th term to be greater than $10\,000.$ Hence,

\begin{align*} 2 \cdot 3^{n - 1} & > 10\,000 \\[5pt] 3^{n - 1} & > 5\,000 \\[5pt] \log \left(3^{n-1}\right) & > \log (5\,000) \\[5pt] (n-1) \log (3) & > \log (5\,000) \\[5pt] n-1 & > \dfrac {\log (5\,000)} {\log (3)} \\[5pt] n & > \dfrac {\log (5\,000)} {\log (3)} +1. \end{align*}

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

\[ \dfrac {\log (5\,000)} {\log (3)}+1 \approx 8.753. \]

Therefore, the $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{9}$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $10\,000.$

question.text: The $6$th term of a geometric sequence is $\dfrac{1}{4}$, and the common ratio is $\dfrac{1}{2}.$ What is the first term of this sequence to be less than $0.001\,2?$
question.explanation:
Since we are given that $a_{6}= \dfrac 1 4$ and $r= \dfrac 1 2$, we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for $a_1$, as follows:

\[ \eqalign{a_n&=a_1\cdot r^{n-1}\\[5pt] a_6&=a_1\cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{6-1}\\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{4}&=a_1\cdot \dfrac{1}{2^5}\\[5pt] \dfrac 1 4&=\dfrac{1}{32} a_1\\[5pt] a_1&=8 } \]

So the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

\[ \begin{align*} a_n & = a_1 \cdot r ^{n -1}\\[3pt] & = 8 \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n - 1}\\[3pt] & = 2^3\cdot 2^{1-n}\\[3pt] & = 2^{4-n}. \end{align*} \]

We want the $n$th term to be less than $0.001\,2.$ Hence:

\[ \begin{align*} 2^{4-n} & < 0.001\,2\\[5pt] \log (2)^{4-n} & < \log (0.001\,2)\\[5pt] (4-n) \log (2) & < \log (0.001\,2)\\[5pt] 4-n & < \dfrac {\log (0.001\,2)} {\log (2)}\\[5pt] -n & < \dfrac {\log (0.001\,2)} {\log (2)} - 4\\[5pt] n & > 4 - \dfrac {\log (0.001\,2)} {\log (2)} \end{align*} \]

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

\[ 4 - \dfrac {\log (0.001\,2)} {\log (2)} \approx 13.703 \]

Therefore, the $14$th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than $0.001\,2.$

question.text: The $6$th term of a geometric sequence is $3$, and the common ratio is $3.$ What is the first term of this sequence to exceed $907?$
question.explanation:
Since we are given that $a_{6}= 3$ and $r=3$, we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for $a_1$, as follows:

\begin{align*} a_n &=a_1\cdot r^{n-1} \\[3pt] a_6 &=a_1\cdot 3^{6-1} \\[3pt] 3 &=a_1\cdot 3^5 \\[3pt] \dfrac{1}{3^4} &= a_1 \\[3pt] a_1 &=\dfrac{1}{81} \end{align*}

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

\begin{align*} a_n & = a_1 \cdot r ^{n -1} \\[3pt] &= \dfrac{1}{81} \cdot 3^{n - 1} \\[3pt] &= 3^{-4}\cdot 3^{n-1} \\[3pt] &= 3^{n-5}. \end{align*}

We want $n$th term to be greater than $907.$ Hence:

\begin{align*} 3^{n - 5} & > 907 \\[5pt] \log \left(3\right)^{n - 5} & > \log (907) \\[5pt] (n - 5) \log \left(3\right) & > \log (907) \\[5pt] n - 5 & > \dfrac {\log (907)} {\log \left(3\right)} \\[5pt] n & > \dfrac {\log (907)} {\log \left(3\right)} + 5 \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

\[ \dfrac {\log (907)} {\log \left(3\right)} + 5 \approx 11.199 \]

Therefore, the $12$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $907.$
